entries.clue: see 28ac.
President, despot – no balls-up put off (9)

indicatorNotes.balls-up: a balls-up is a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

annotation.surface: A despotic president's plans come to nothing through a cock-up.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash hides that 'no' belongs with 'despot' as fodder rather than negating 'balls-up'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: postponing a meeting and putting it off are the same delay.

entries.clue: Let Nigel finally moderate (5)

indicatorNotes.finally: takes the final letter of Nigel

annotation.surface: A plea to allow Nigel (Farage, presumably) to tone things down at last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Let' reads as a command opening the sentence; it is the definition, as in 'let a flat'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the property sense: landlords let or lease a flat to a tenant.

entries.clue: Naturally, welcoming Fed chief is probably not Trump's preferred situation (3,6)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: the outer phrase takes in a guest
indicatorNotes.chief: the head, or first letter, of Fed

blocks.note: the rest of OF COURSE, which takes in the F

annotation.surface: A remark on the Federal Reserve chairman and Trump's discomfort at having to meet him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Naturally' looks like a throwaway adverb, but it is OF COURSE. Trump is a keen golfer, so being off the course is not where he likes to be.
annotation.definitionFit: Trump loves the golf course, so being off course is probably not his favoured spot.

entries.clue: Fake news ending, "contained in strong beer" (5)

indicatorNotes.ending: takes the final letter of news
indicatorNotes.contained in: the S goes inside the next part

blocks.note: f (forte) is the musical mark for loud or strong
end of ALE, around the S

annotation.surface: A fake news story ending with a quote about a pub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fake news' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Fake' alone and 'news' supplies its last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a fake passport is a false one, not what it claims to be.

entries.clue: OBN candidate, babe who wants to go places? (7)

annotation.definition2: babe who wants to go places?

blocks.note: a sycophant, fit for Private Eye's Order of the Brown Nose

blocks.clueFragment: babe who wants to go places?
blocks.note: a baby on all fours, on the move

annotation.surface: An ambitious young thing angling for honours by flattering the powerful.
annotation.walkthrough: OBN is Private Eye's mock honour, the Order of the Brown Nose, given to shameless flatterers. 'Wants to go places' sounds like ambition, but the babe is a baby learning to move.
annotation.definitionFit: A crawler is a toady who sucks up, and also a baby that has started crawling.

entries.clue: Out-and-out Trump subordinate heading off comment (9)

indicatorNotes.heading off: the head, or first letter, is removed

blocks.note: VANCE, the US Vice President, without the V

annotation.surface: A complete Trump underling heading off to avoid giving a comment.
annotation.walkthrough: JD Vance is Trump's Vice President, so he is the subordinate who loses his head.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any remark spoken aloud counts as an utterance.

entries.clue: Jagger's cosying up to Blair? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: Jagger is a Stone, one of the Rolling Stones, rather than a synonym for the word.

indicatorNotes.cosying up to: the S snuggles right next to the following piece

annotation.surface: Mick Jagger getting friendly with Tony Blair.
annotation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was often matily called 'Tone'; the apostrophe S is lifted straight from 'Jagger's' and set beside him.
annotation.definitionFit: Mick Jagger is a Stone, frontman of the Rolling Stones.

entries.clue: Society in old Elizabeth I's rule (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places Society inside the next piece, so the S sits within Bess

blocks.note: first letter of BESS, which will hold the S
rest of BESS, pet name of Elizabeth I

annotation.surface: A history note on court society under the reign of Elizabeth I.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rule' looks like the monarch's reign, but it is a verb: to dominate one's thoughts. Elizabeth I was known as Good Queen Bess.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that obsesses you rules your mind.

entries.clue: Bust ruptured with nail? Capital! (8)

indicatorNotes.ruptured: the letters are broken apart and reformed

annotation.surface: A statue's bust smashed with a nail, greeted with a cry of 'Excellent!'
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' reads as an old-fashioned cry of approval. Istanbul was the capital of the Ottoman Empire, which is why the exclamation mark hedges.
annotation.definitionFit: Istanbul was long the capital of the Byzantine and Ottoman empires.

entries.clue: Lawsuit makes e.g. Momentum F-off (6)

indicatorNotes.off: 'F-off' reads as an insult, but taking the F off a word literally removes that letter

blocks.note: FACTION, as Momentum is a Labour faction, less F

annotation.surface: A legal challenge to the Labour group Momentum, told where to go.
annotation.walkthrough: Momentum is a left-wing group within the Labour Party, an example of a faction. 'F-off' reads as an insult but instructs you to drop the F.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal term: bringing a lawsuit is formally bringing an action in court.

entries.clue: Patchy article on male "transitional" (9)

indicatorNotes.transitional: the letters are in transition to a new order

blocks.note: a piece is an article, as in a newspaper

annotation.surface: A critique of a scrappy newspaper article about a trans man.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'transitional' make it look like a quoted word; it is the anagram indicator acting on 'male'.
annotation.definitionFit: Piecemeal, done bit by bit, is patchy.

entries.clue: Key Republican charge is repelled (4)

annotation.surface: A vital Republican accusation is fought off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like an adjective meaning important, but it is a noun: a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
annotation.definitionFit: A key (or cay) is a low island or reef.

entries.clue: God's book hijacked by USA in turmoil (6)

indicatorNotes.hijacked by: the B is seized and held inside the other letters

blocks.note: first part of USA IN rearranged

annotation.surface: The Bible being taken over by a chaotic America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link inside the phrase, but it is anagram fodder alongside USA.
annotation.definitionFit: Anubis is the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead.

entries.clue: Support Hunt – make a U-turn (9)

annotation.surface: Politicians urged to back Jeremy Hunt and change course.
annotation.walkthrough: Capital H makes 'Hunt' look like Jeremy Hunt, the Tory politician; it is just the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a politician's U-turn is reversing course, retracing steps already taken.

entries.clue: Title: "Pub Reversed Net Zero" (7)

indicatorNotes.Reversed: swaps the order of the two words Net and Zero, not their letters

annotation.surface: A headline: a pub has turned its back on net zero.
annotation.walkthrough: Here 'Reversed' swaps the two words, putting Zero before Net; reversing the letters would give nothing useful.
annotation.definitionFit: A baronet is a hereditary title, below a baron.

entries.clue: Stuck up character after bishop's seat (3)

indicatorNotes.Stuck up: in a down clue, raised up means written bottom to top
indicatorNotes.after: the reversed letters come after the B

annotation.surface: A snooty type angling for a bishop's seat in the Lords.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up character' reads as a snob, but the character is a Greek letter and it is stuck upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: Your bum is what you sit on, your seat.

entries.clue: Yank and the flustered Tory leadership contender (9)

indicatorNotes.flustered: the letters are thrown into confusion

annotation.surface: An American and a rattled Conservative hopeful.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American; it is the verb. Tom Tugendhat stood for the Conservative leadership in 2022 and 2024.
annotation.definitionFit: Tom Tugendhat, a Conservative MP, ran for the party leadership.

entries.clue: Kinky medical spout (7)

indicatorNotes.Kinky: something kinky is bent or twisted, so the letters of medical come out bent into a new order

annotation.surface: Some unconventional kit found in a doctor's surgery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like a noun, a nozzle on medical equipment; it is the verb, to hold forth.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a sneer: to spout is to hold forth pompously, as an orator declaims.

entries.clue: American second-rate party guys from which shit originates (7)

annotation.surface: A scathing verdict on a poor-quality American frat party as the source of all the trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition takes 'shit' literally, though the surface uses it as slang for rubbish.
annotation.definitionFit: Faeces are produced in the gut, housed in the abdomen.

entries.clue: Medic on the brink – look for a body! (6)

annotation.surface: A doctor at breaking point, urged to find a patient or a corpse.
annotation.walkthrough: Police dredge rivers and lakes when searching for a drowned body.
annotation.definitionFit: Dredging a river bed is how a missing body is often searched for.

entries.clue: Courting lawyer takes money, quite a bit of money (6)

blocks.note: a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

annotation.surface: A lawyer paid handsomely for courting a client, or a rich partner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Takes' just puts the money after the lawyer; G for grand is a common abbreviation for a thousand.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: courting is the old-fashioned word for going out with someone.

entries.clue: Sex just started to get glib for Barney (4)

indicatorNotes.just started: only the start, the first letter, of sex

blocks.note: a pat answer is a glib one

annotation.surface: Someone called Barney smoothly talking his way into bed.
annotation.walkthrough: Barney looks like a name; it is British slang for a row or quarrel.
annotation.definitionFit: A British slang synonym: a barney is a noisy squabble, and so is a spat.

entries.clue: Pressure put on press – Russian leader's action? (5)

annotation.surface: Putin cracking down on the media.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests pressure on journalists; the definition points at Stalin's purges, by example, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: Russian leaders, Stalin above all, are notorious for purging rivals.

entries.clue: Balls twisted on faulty latch – no contest (9)

indicatorNotes.faulty: the letters are broken and reordered

blocks.note: ED Balls, the politician turned broadcaster

annotation.surface: A mishap with a broken lock that ends a match before it starts.
annotation.walkthrough: Ed Balls is a former Labour minister, now a TV presenter. 'No contest' looks like a phrase, but 'no' is fodder and 'contest' the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A decathlon is a ten-event athletics contest.

entries.clue: Herb's about, er, to get elected (5)

annotation.surface: A hesitant candidate named Herb who is about to win a seat.
annotation.walkthrough: Herb reads as a man's name; it is the plant. Cumin is really a spice, but the plant is a herb.
annotation.definitionFit: Cumin is a plant of the parsley family, grown for its seeds.

entries.clue: Tempt with a kiss and glam wear? (5)

blocks.note: X is a kiss at the end of a letter

annotation.surface: Seduction advice: a kiss and something sparkly to wear.
annotation.walkthrough: Lurex is a trade name for a glittery metallic yarn woven into party clothes; the question mark allows for defining a fabric as clothing.
annotation.definitionFit: Lurex is sparkly metallic fabric, the stuff of glam outfits.

entries.clue: Alternative fuel must start coming (6)

indicatorNotes.start: the start, or first letter, of must

annotation.surface: An energy policy promise: green fuels must be introduced soon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coming' looks like 'on the way', echoing the energy surface; it is the sexual sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense: 'coming' in the sexual sense means reaching climax.

entries.clue: Our nation's anchor – casually dumped in well (8)

indicatorNotes.casually: the letters are arranged at random

blocks.note: first letter of MY, an exclamation like 'well!'
end of MY, around the rearranged letters

annotation.surface: Britain's steadying anchor has been carelessly thrown down a well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Well' reads as a water shaft, but it is the exclamation 'My!'. The UK is a monarchy.
annotation.definitionFit: Britain, 'our nation' to a British setter, is a monarchy.

entries.clue: Bill's final judgement? (9)

blocks.note: a bill in the older sense: an account to be settled
the Last Judgement, when all accounts are settled

annotation.surface: A man named Bill faces his final verdict.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a name, or a parliamentary bill; it is a bill to pay, an old sense of reckoning.
annotation.definitionFit: A reckoning is an account or bill, and the day of reckoning is the Last Judgement.

entries.clue: (& 1ac.) Parrot's gone to meet its maker – early indication of who'll get in? (4)

annotation.definition: early indication of who'll get in?

blocks.note: an exit is a death, a departure from the stage of life
Poll (Polly) is the stock name for a parrot

annotation.surface: Monty Python's dead parrot sketch, retold as election-night news.
annotation.walkthrough: The parrot comes first in the clue but last in the answer: the 's makes it 'Parrot has gone', and the dead bird's exit is written ahead of its name.
annotation.definitionFit: An exit poll, taken as voters leave, is the first sign on election night of who has won a seat.
